en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Surāpānavagga 60.
The Training Rule on the Storing of Robes.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of seventeen monks were without stored requisites.
The group of six monks stole even the bowls and robes of the group of seventeen monks.
The group of seventeen monks said this to the group of six monks:
“Give us, friends, our bowl and robe as well.
The group-of-six monks laughed; they wept.
The monks said this:
“Friends, why are you weeping?
“Friend, these monks of the group-of-six are even snatching away our bowls and robes.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant.
“How indeed can the group of six monks hide away even the bowls and robes of other monks?
… [after the usual inquiry] … “Is it true, monks, that you hide away even the bowls and robes of other monks?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, take away even the bowl or the robe of the monks?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:

“Whosoever, however, a monk should hide, or cause to be hidden, another monk’s bowl, or robe, or sitting mat, or needle case, or girdle—even if only in jest—it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Whosoever, however:
Whoever is such a person … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
"Of a bhikkhu" means of another bhikkhu. "Alms-bowl" (patto) is as follows: [text continues].
There are two kinds of bowls: an iron bowl and a clay bowl.
What is called "robe" refers to any one of the six kinds of robes; the last one is that which is subject to formal assignment.
A sitting mat is called "with a border.
A needle case is called...
With a needle or without a needle.
"Girdle" means there are two kinds of girdles: the woven band and the pig-girth.
"Or she should direct [it] away herself":
if she directs it away herself, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"Or she should cause it to be directed away":...
If he commands another, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, having been commanded once, he removes even much [of the robe-material], there is an offense of expiation.
This applies even if it is done merely for the sake of a joke.
With the intention to play:

if one perceives a person as fully ordained and either hides or causes another to hide a bowl, a robe, a sitting mat, a needle case, or a waistband—even if only for the sake of a joke—one incurs an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If one is in doubt regarding whether the person is fully ordained... [and so forth].

If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as not being fully ordained, and one hides or causes another to hide his bowl, robe, sitting mat, needle case, or waistband—even if only for the sake of a joke—one commits an offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*).
If one hides or causes another to hide any other requisite—even if only for the sake of a joke—one commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

If one hides or causes another to hide the bowl, robe, or any other requisite belonging to a person who is not fully ordained—even if only for the sake of a joke—one commits an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives someone who is not fully ordained as being fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one is uncertain regarding someone who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives someone who is not fully ordained as being not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if he does not intend to hide it,
or if he puts away what was poorly placed.
If one puts it away [thinking], “I will give it after giving a Dhamma talk,” there is no offense for one who is insane or for an initial offender.
The tenth training rule concerning the storage of robes is finished.
This is the sixth chapter on the drinking of fermented liquor.
Its summary verse:
Alcohol, laughing with the fingers,
disrespect, and causing alarm;
lighting a fire, bathing, and [using] discolored [water].
And by means of conciliation and by means of removal.
